notes.meaning: Satan used a real serpent as his tool to tempt Eve. He started by asking a sly question to make God's rule seem harsh and unfair, planting the idea that God was holding back good things from them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The serpent's cleverness targets the couple's innocence, setting up a contrast between the humans who start out naked and unashamed and the clever serpent who ends up cursed.

notes.meaning: Eve answered the serpent by explaining that God gave them great freedom to eat from the trees in the garden. Even so, she began to talk with the tempter instead of turning away from danger immediately.

Eve described the tree in the middle of the garden, saying God warned them not to eat or touch it, or they would die. By adding the rule about not touching it, she showed that she was beginning to view God's command as overly strict, and her trust in His warning was starting to weaken.
The serpent bluntly told the woman that she would not die. He openly called God a liar, trying to remove her fear of punishment so that sin would seem completely safe.

The serpent claimed God was holding them back from becoming like Him in knowing good and evil. He tempted Eve with the pride of gaining higher wisdom and independence, making God look jealous and unkind.

Eve looked at the fruit, saw that it looked delicious and desirable for gaining wisdom, and ate it. She gave some to her husband, and he ate it as well, choosing outright disobedience against his Creator.

differ.view: Adam was likely not with Eve when she was tempted, but joined her later and ate because she urged him to.
Adam stood right beside Eve during the conversation, watching silently before choosing to eat with his eyes wide open.

notes.meaning: Their eyes opened, but only to realize their own guilt and shame. Seeing that their innocence was gone and that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together to make coverings.

Adam and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden during the cool evening breeze. Instead of welcoming God with joy as they had done before, their guilty consciences made them run and hide among the trees.
The Lord God called out to Adam, asking where he was. God did not ask because He lacked information, but to tenderly search out the lost sinner and prompt him to face his fallen state.
Adam answered that he hid because he heard God's voice and felt afraid of his nakedness. He admitted his fear and shame, but he still avoided confessing the real sin of breaking God's command.

God asked Adam who told him he was naked and whether he had eaten from the forbidden tree. This direct question forced Adam to look at God's clear commandment and see that his shame came from his own disobedience.
Adam admitted that he ate the fruit, but he blamed his wife for handing it to him. By pointing out that God had given him the woman, Adam also tried to shift the blame onto God.
God asked the woman what she had done, and she admitted that she ate the fruit. Instead of truly humbling herself, she blamed the serpent for tricking her with lies.

God passed sentence on the serpent without asking it any questions, since it was already rebellious and offered no hope of repentance. The creature was cursed above all animals, condemned to crawl on its belly and eat dust as a sign of complete dishonor.

God declared lifelong warfare between the devil and the woman, and between their followers. The woman's offspring points to Jesus Christ, who would suffer in His human nature when His heel was bruised on the cross, but would crush Satan's head and win the final victory.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: This verse is seen as the earliest prophecy of Mary, who shares in the battle against the devil and crushes him indirectly through her Son.

notes.meaning: God told the woman that pregnancy and giving birth would now bring great physical pain and distress. She was also placed in a position of humble subjection under her husband's leadership.

differ.view: The woman's natural desires are made subject to her husband's will, placing her under his lawful authority.
The woman's desire refers to a urge to control or master her husband, leading to ongoing struggle within marriage.

notes.meaning: God rebuked Adam for following his wife instead of his Creator and cursed the ground because of him. From now on, farming and earning a living would be filled with pain, sorrow, and tiring work for the rest of his days.
The ground would no longer produce food easily, but would sprout thorns and weeds that choke good crops. Adam would have to work hard to gather and grow plants from the field to survive.

Adam would have to work hard to eat bread by the sweat of his brow until the day he died. Because he was formed from the ground, physical death would turn his body back into dust as the final penalty for sin.

Adam named his wife Eve, which means life, because she would become the mother of every living person. This showed his faith in God's promise that life would continue and that a Savior would eventually be born through her.

The Lord God showed mercy by making durable coats of animal skin to replace their fragile fig leaves. Slaying these animals was an early picture of sacrifice, showing that life had to be given so guilty sinners could be covered.

God noted that man had learned the difference between good and evil, but only through the bitter experience of rebellion and misery. To keep Adam from eating from the tree of life and living forever in an unending, fallen state, God determined to remove him.

The Lord God sent man out of the garden of Eden to farm the ordinary ground from which he was taken. Adam was sent to a place of hard labor, yet God mercifully spared his life and continued to provide him with food.

God drove the man out and placed cherubim, powerful heavenly beings, along with a flashing sword of fire to guard the path to the tree of life. This barred humans from trying to earn eternal life on their own terms, pointing them instead to salvation through the promised Savior.
